title: The same regex in Python and JavaScript
summary: Python's re (raw strings, match versus search versus fullmatch, findall's groups) and JavaScript's RegExp (flags, lastIndex, matchAll, named groups), with the bug each one is famous for, then a port to C#.

steps.title: Python: re in five calls
body: Python's `re` module is close to .NET, with different names. Always write patterns as **raw strings**
`r"..."`, so Python leaves the backslashes alone.
```python
import re
TICKET = re.compile(r"[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+")          # compile once at module level, reuse
re.search(r"\d+", "id 42")       # first match ANYWHERE      -> <re.Match ... match='42'>
re.match(r"\d+", "id 42")        # only at the START         -> None
re.fullmatch(r"\d+", "42")       # the WHOLE string          -> a match: use this to validate
for m in TICKET.finditer(text):   # Match objects: m.group(), m.start(), m["name"]
print(m.group())
re.sub(r"\d+", lambda m: str(int(m.group()) + 1), "v1.9")   # 'v2.10'
- Named groups are `(?P<name>...)`; Python's `re` does not accept .NET's `(?<name>...)`.
- `re.VERBOSE` (`re.X`) is .NET's IgnorePatternWhitespace. Python 3.11+ also has atomic groups and possessive
quantifiers.
- **`findall` changes shape with groups**: no group gives the matched strings, one group gives that group's
text, several groups give tuples. The whole match is gone as soon as you add a group.

steps.prompt: A Python API must reject anything that is not exactly a ticket key, such as `OPS-311`. Which call does that?
steps.explain: `re.match` only anchors the **start**: it accepts `OPS-311; DROP TABLE`. `re.search` accepts a key anywhere. `fullmatch` requires the whole string, like `^...\Z` (or `\A...\z` in .NET).
No group: whole matches. Two groups: a tuple per match. One group: just that group, and the numbers are gone. When you need the whole match and the groups, use `finditer`.

steps.title: Symptom: the release script prints tuples
prompt: **Symptom.** A Python release script runs `re.findall(r"v(\d+)\.(\d+)(\.\d+)?", notes)` and the changelog
Rewrite the pattern so it matches the same versions but has **no capturing groups**, so `findall` returns
whole matches. (The checks run in .NET, which treats groups the same way here.)

all.input: ships v1.2 and v2.10.3, not v3

forbid.message: Has no capturing groups (use (?:...) to group)

hints: The first two groups are not needed at all: `v\d+\.\d+(?:\.\d+)?`.
steps.explain: With no capturing group, `findall` returns whole matches. The optional patch still needs a group for `?` to apply to, so make it non-capturing. In .NET, `RegexOptions.ExplicitCapture` does the same for a whole pattern.

steps.title: JavaScript: literals, flags and lastIndex
body: In JavaScript a regex is usually a **literal**: `/pattern/flags`, so there is no string escaping at all.
```typescript
const ticket = /\b[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+\b/g;
ticket.test(s);                                // boolean
s.match(/(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d\d)/)?.groups?.y;  // first match; named groups on .groups
for (const m of s.matchAll(ticket)) {}         // every match (m[0], m.index); needs the g flag
s.replace(/(?<u>\w+)@(\w+)/, "$<u> at $2");     // first match only, unless the regex has g
s.replaceAll(/\d+/g, n => String(Number(n) + 1)); // with a regex, replaceAll requires g
Flags: `g` global, `i`, `m`, `s` (dot matches newlines), `u` Unicode, `v` (ES2024: Unicode sets, such as
`[\p{L}--[a-z]]`), `y` sticky, `d` (indices of every group in `m.indices`).
**The trap:** a regex with `g` or `y` is **stateful**. `test()` and `exec()` start searching at
`regex.lastIndex` and move it forward after a match. Reuse such a regex on another string, and it starts
in the middle.
New in ES2025: `RegExp.escape(text)` (Node 24+), inline modifiers like `(?i:abc)`, and the same group name
in different alternatives.

steps.prompt: A filter keeps the error lines. What does this JavaScript print?
steps.explain: The first `test` matches and sets `lastIndex` to 5. The second starts at position 5 of `"error 2"`, finds nothing, returns false and resets `lastIndex` to 0. So the results alternate: true, false, true, false. A classic production bug: it only shows up with several inputs in a row.

steps.prompt: How do you fix the filter so it keeps all four lines? Select all that apply.
steps.explain: `g` only makes sense for `matchAll`, `replace` and `replaceAll`; a yes-or-no test should not have it. Resetting `lastIndex` also works but is easy to forget. `y` (sticky) also uses `lastIndex`, and anchors the search there, so it makes things worse.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: regex APIs in three languages
steps.body: The calls experienced engineers reach for when a regex goes into code, and the option on each that prevents the classic bug.

toolkit.cmd:
[GeneratedRegex(@"^[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+$", RegexOptions.CultureInvariant, matchTimeoutMilliseconds: 250)]
private static partial Regex TicketKey();
toolkit.what: C#: the default for a pattern known at build time. Generated at compile time, no startup cost, works with Native AOT; analyzer SYSLIB1045 suggests it.
flags: with IgnoreCase: the same answer on every machine (the Turkish i)
toolkit.when: every fixed pattern in production C#

toolkit.cmd: foreach (ValueMatch m in regex.EnumerateMatches(text)) total += m.Length;
toolkit.what: C#: scan without allocating a Match per hit (.NET 7+). Regex.Count(text) counts the same way.
flags: index and length only, no allocation
toolkit.when: hot paths: log ingestion, request filters

toolkit.what: Python: compile once at module level, always with a raw string r"...".
flags: the whole string must match (use it to validate)
only anchors the start, a common validation bug
Match objects, not the tuples findall gives with groups
spaces and # comments in the pattern
toolkit.example: pairs = {m['key']: m['value'] for m in PATTERN.finditer(line)}

toolkit.cmd:
const re = /(?<key>\w+)=(?<value>\S+)/g;
for (const m of line.matchAll(re)) map.set(m.groups.key, m.groups.value);
toolkit.what: JavaScript: matchAll for every match with groups. A /g regex keeps lastIndex, so never reuse one with test() across strings.
flags: global: needed by matchAll and replaceAll
toolkit.example: const isTicket = /^[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+$/.test(input);   // no g flag on a validator
toolkit.when: front ends, Node services, build scripts

steps.prompt: Match each JavaScript feature to what it does.
pairs: every match as an iterator; a TypeError without the `g` flag
`m.indices`: start and end of the match and of each group
set operations in classes, such as `[\p{L}--[a-z]]`
the text of a named group
a named group inside a replacement string

steps.prompt: Which language does each piece of syntax belong to?
steps.explain: `(?<name>...)` works in .NET and JavaScript but not in Python's `re`. JavaScript has no flag for comments in a pattern at all.

steps.title: Port a Python pattern to .NET
prompt: A Python validator uses `(?P<key>[a-z_]+)=(?P<val>\d+)` for settings like `max_conn=40`. .NET does not accept
`(?P<`. Write the .NET pattern with the same two group names, matching a whole setting.
hints: Only the group syntax changes: `(?P<key>...)` becomes `(?<key>...)`.
steps.explain: Most of a pattern ports unchanged. What differs is group syntax, flags and edge cases: `\d` matches all Unicode digits in .NET and Python, but only `0-9` in JavaScript; `$` without the m flag accepts a final newline in .NET and Python, but not in JavaScript.

steps.title: Port the JavaScript log parser to C#
prompt: The browser client summarises log lines like this:
Port it to C# so the server gives the **same** answers. Write `static partial class LogLine` with a
source-generated regex and `public static string? Summary(string line)`.
One difference matters: in JavaScript, `$` without the m flag only matches at the very end, so a line with a
trailing `\n` gives `null`. In .NET, `$` also matches before a final `\n`. End the .NET pattern with `\z`.
template: Dojo.Eq("an ERROR line", "ERROR: disk full", LogLine.Summary("2026-11-26T09:12:04Z ERROR disk full"));
Dojo.Eq("an INFO line", "INFO: ok", LogLine.Summary("2026-11-26T09:12:05Z INFO ok"));
Dojo.Check("not a log line gives null", LogLine.Summary("not a log line") is null, "expected null");
Dojo.Check("a trailing newline gives null, as in JavaScript", LogLine.Summary("2026-11-26T09:12:04Z ERROR disk full\n") is null, "expected null: end the pattern with \\z");
Dojo.Check("two lines give null, as in JavaScript", LogLine.Summary("2026-11-26T09:12:04Z ERROR first\nsecond") is null, "expected null");
